medium.title: Lemur
medium.line: Clade of primates endemic to the island of Madagascar

medium.text: Lemurs are wet-nosed primates of the superfamily Lemuroidea, divided into eight families and consisting of 15 genera and around 100 extant species.

medium.caption: Before the arrival of humans roughly 1500 to 2000 years ago, lemurs were found all across the island.

medium.text: Most existing lemurs are small, with a pointed snout, large eyes, and a long tail.
Lemurs share resemblance with other primates, but evolved independently from monkeys and apes.
In addition, conservation organizations increasingly seek to implement community-based approaches to save lemur species and promote sustainability.

deep.title: Lemur
deep.line: Clade of primates endemic to the island of Madagascar

deep.text: Lemurs are wet-nosed primates of the superfamily Lemuroidea, divided into eight families and consisting of 15 genera and around 100 extant species.

deep.caption: Since the arrival of humans on the island around 2,000 years ago, over a dozen species of “giant lemurs” larger than living lemur species have become extinct, including the gorilla-sized Archaeoindris.

deep.text: Most existing lemurs are small, with a pointed snout, large eyes, and a long tail.
Carl Linnaeus, the founder of modern binomial nomenclature, gave lemurs their name as early as 1758.
Lemurs are primates belonging to the suborder Strepsirrhini.
All modern strepsirrhines including lemurs are traditionally thought to have evolved from early primates known as adapiforms during the Eocene or Paleocene.
Lemurs have adapted to fill many open ecological niches since making their way to Madagascar.

Ranging in size from the 30 g Madame Berthe’s mouse lemur, the world’s smallest primate, to the recently extinct 160–200 kg Archaeoindris fontoynonti, lemurs evolved diverse forms of locomotion, varying levels of social complexity.
Before the arrival of humans roughly 1500 to 2000 years ago, lemurs were found all across the island.
In addition, conservation organizations increasingly seek to implement community-based approaches to save lemur species and promote sustainability.
